items.followUp: A force of 150 N acts perpendicular to a surface of area 3 m². Find the pressure in pascals.

rubric.why: Identifies the equivalence between the pascal and the SI unit of pressure.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equivalence.

rubric.why: Defines one pascal using the force and area that produce it.
rubric.description: Define one pascal as the pressure produced by a perpendicular force of 1 N acting on an area of 1 m².
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for including the force, area, and perpendicular direction.

modelAnswer: Yes, 1 N m⁻² = 1 Pa.
One pascal is the pressure produced when a perpendicular force of 1 N acts on an area of 1 m².

items.followUp: Explain why water rises through a straw when a person sucks air from it.

rubric.why: Recognises that sucking lowers the pressure inside the straw.
rubric.description: State that sucking reduces the pressure inside the straw.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the pressure inside the straw becomes lower.

rubric.why: Identifies atmospheric pressure as what pushes the liquid up the straw.
rubric.description: Explain that atmospheric pressure acting on the liquid surface pushes the liquid upward.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the role of atmospheric pressure in raising the liquid.

modelAnswer: When we suck air from the straw, the pressure inside the straw becomes lower than atmospheric pressure.
Atmospheric pressure acting on the liquid surface pushes the liquid up the straw and into the mouth.

items.followUp: A perpendicular force of 120 N is applied to a wrench 25 cm from its pivot. Find the torque and state its direction if the force acts upward at the left end.

rubric.why: Uses the perpendicular distance from the pivot in SI units.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating the correct SI distance.

rubric.why: Applies the torque relation and gives the correct magnitude and direction.
rubric.description: Calculate τ = Fd = 200 N × 0.20 m = 40 N m and state that the torque is clockwise.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct torque calculation and result; the stated direction is included in the model answer.

modelAnswer: Given: F = 200 N; perpendicular distance, d = 20 cm = 0.20 m.
Formula: τ = Fd.
Substitution: τ = 200 N × 0.20 m = 40 N m.
The torque is 40 N m, clockwise about the pivot.

items.followUp: Define equilibrium and give an example of a body in static equilibrium.

rubric.why: States the zero-resultant-force condition for equilibrium.
rubric.description: Define equilibrium as the state in which the resultant force on a body is zero.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the resultant or net force is zero.

rubric.why: Gives a moving body whose velocity is constant, so it is in equilibrium.
rubric.description: Give a suitable moving-body example, such as a car moving in a straight line at constant velocity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid moving-body example.

modelAnswer: A body is in equilibrium when the resultant force acting on it is zero.
A car moving in a straight line at constant velocity is an example of a moving body in equilibrium.

items.followUp: Find the gravitational potential energy of a 4 kg body raised 8 m above the ground. Take g = 10 m s⁻².

rubric.why: Identifies the mass and height in SI units and states the value of gravitational acceleration used.
rubric.description: State m = 10 kg, h = 5 m, and use g = 9.8 m s⁻² (or approximately 10 m s⁻²).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correctly stated data and a suitable value of g.

rubric.why: Uses gravitational potential energy correctly and evaluates it with a consistent value of g.
rubric.description: Calculate GPE = mgh, giving 490 J with g = 9.8 m s⁻² or 500 J with g = 10 m s⁻².
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct formula, substitution, and answer with unit using a consistent value of g.

modelAnswer: Given: m = 10 kg; h = 5 m; g = 9.8 m s⁻².
Formula: GPE = mgh.
Substitution: GPE = 10 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² × 5 m.
Answer: GPE = 490 J.

items.followUp: What is the SI unit of energy? Define one joule.

rubric.why: Names the SI unit of power.
rubric.description: State that the SI unit of power is the watt (W).
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct unit.

rubric.why: Defines one watt as a rate of doing work and relates it to joules per second.
rubric.description: Define one watt as the power when 1 J of work is done in 1 s.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition of the watt.

modelAnswer: The SI unit of power is the watt (W).
One watt is the power of a body that does 1 J of work in 1 s; 1 W = 1 J s⁻¹.

items.followUp: State the law of conservation of momentum and show, using a collision between two bodies, that total momentum is conserved.

rubric.why: States the conservation law and its condition.
rubric.description: State that the total momentum of an isolated system remains constant if no external force acts on it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the law with the isolated-system or no-external-force condition.

rubric.why: Uses Newton’s third law to relate the interaction forces during collision.
rubric.description: State that the collision forces are equal and opposite, by Newton’s third law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the equal-and-opposite force relationship.

rubric.why: Derives the equality of total momentum before and after collision.
rubric.description: Show the momentum equation m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂, or a valid preceding equation that leads to it.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct equation or derivation.

rubric.why: Verifies conservation with a numerical collision example.
rubric.description: Give a consistent example in which total momentum before and after collision is the same.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct numerical verification with momentum units.

modelAnswer: Law: If no external force acts on a system, its total momentum remains constant.
Consider two bodies of masses m₁ and m₂ colliding; let their velocities before collision be u₁ and u₂ and after collision be v₁ and v₂.
During the collision, F₁ = m₁(v₁ − u₁)/t and F₂ = m₂(v₂ − u₂)/t.
The collision forces are equal and opposite (F₁ = −F₂), by Newton’s third law.
Therefore, m₁(v₁ − u₁) = −m₂(v₂ − u₂), so m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂.
Example: let m₁ = 2 kg, u₁ = 3 m s⁻¹, m₂ = 1 kg, and u₂ = 0; after collision let v₁ = 1 m s⁻¹ and v₂ = 4 m s⁻¹.
Momentum before = (2 × 3) + (1 × 0) = 6 kg m s⁻¹; momentum after = (2 × 1) + (1 × 4) = 6 kg m s⁻¹.
Thus, total momentum before the collision equals total momentum after it.
